idea.why: One analyst per data domain, an editor that merges and cross-references, then a deterministic render and a delivery step. The model produces only content; the chrome is fixed by a template node, so a bad generation degrades the copy and not the page. Loses points because the briefing exists solely as an email payload.

structure.why: Right node types throughout, and one model feeding all three agents avoids triplicate ceremony. The gap is a missing guard on the one node whose output is parsed structurally: the editor must emit a clean fragment with no parser or sanitise step behind it, so a stray code fence lands verbatim in the dashboard.

connections.why: The one visibly weak dimension. Two wholly independent fetches are chained, giving a depth of five for a depth-three problem. The middle edge carries no data, only ordering, and the real join is smuggled in through node references instead of a merge.

answer.why: End to end and recognisable, with disciplined prompts about not inventing senders or events. Held back by the delivery medium: the stylesheet sits after the closing html tag and the layout relies on grid, neither of which survives most mail clients.

appraisal: This finds the right shape: two domain analysts each owning one source and one tool, an editor that merges and cross-references, and a deterministic template that keeps page chrome out of the model's hands. Node choices are disciplined, particularly the template node rather than a Code node and a single shared model. The wiring is where it falls down: two unrelated fetches are serialised into a chain whose middle edge carries no data at all, and the real join is smuggled through node references instead of a merge. A knowledgeable user would fix that first, then the presentation, since a grid layout and a stylesheet placed outside the document will not render in Gmail.
